diag.1: No permanent dipole — C–H bonds and the symmetric chain leave the molecule essentially nonpolar.
diag.2: H-bonding requires H attached to N, O, or F.
diag.3: Ion-dipole needs a dissolved ion; pure hexane has none.

question: Dominant IMF in liquid acetone?
why: Acetone has a strong C=O dipole but no H attached to O, N, or F — so dipole-dipole, not H-bonding, is dominant.

diag.0: Polar C=O bond rules out London-only.
diag.2: Acetone is an H-bond acceptor (lone pairs on O), but it has no donor — so it cannot self-H-bond.
diag.3: No ions present in pure acetone.

question: Dominant IMF in liquid ethanol?
why: Ethanol's O—H is both H-bond donor and acceptor, giving it a much higher boiling point than its dipole-only analogs.

diag.0: London is always present, but H-bonding dominates here because of the polar O—H.
diag.1: Dipole-dipole alone wouldn't capture the much stronger O—H···O network.
diag.3: No ions in pure ethanol.

question: What's the dominant interaction holding Na⁺ in aqueous solution?
why: Na⁺ aligns the negative end (O) of each water dipole toward itself — this charge–dipole interaction is ion-dipole, the strongest non-bonded force besides ion-ion.

diag.0: London is far weaker than the charge–dipole pull from a full positive ion.
diag.1: Dipole-dipole is between two neutral polar molecules; here one species is charged.
diag.2: Water can H-bond to other waters, but the Na⁺/H₂O interaction itself is ion-dipole, not H-bond.

question: HF has a much higher boiling point than HI despite being lighter. Why?
options: Heavier atoms always raise boiling point
London dispersion is stronger in HF
Hydrogen bonding in HF outweighs HI's larger London force
why: F is small + highly electronegative, so HF forms strong H-bonds. HI has stronger London (more polarizable I) but no H-bonding — H-bonds win here.

diag.0: Trend reversed: HI is heavier yet boils lower; H-bonding overrides the mass effect.
diag.1: Wrong direction — HI is more polarizable and has the larger London force.
diag.3: HI is polar (Δχ ≈ 0.5).

question: Hybridization of the central carbon?
why: Four electron domains (all single bonds) on a 2nd-row atom is sp³. Methane is the canonical example.

diag.0: sp would imply 2 electron domains (linear geometry).
diag.1: sp² has 3 domains (trigonal planar).
diag.3: sp³d needs a 3rd-period or later atom; carbon cannot expand its octet.

question: Hybridization of each carbon in ethene (C₂H₄)?
why: Each carbon has 3 σ bonds (2 C—H + 1 C—C), and the π bond uses the unhybridized p orbital — three domains means sp².

diag.0: sp would mean linear with 2 σ bonds; ethene's carbons have 3 σ bonds each.
diag.2: sp³ predicts 4 σ; ethene only has 3 σ per carbon.
diag.3: sp³d needs an expanded octet — not possible for a 2nd-row C.

question: Hybridization of each carbon in acetylene (HC≡CH)?
why: Each C makes 2 σ bonds (1 C—H + 1 C—C). The two π bonds use the remaining unhybridized p orbitals — sp.

diag.1: sp² predicts 3 σ bonds; acetylene's carbons only have 2.
diag.2: sp³ predicts 4 σ bonds.
diag.3: sp³d² is octahedral; carbon cannot expand its octet.

why: Five electron domains around P (period 3) require expanded-octet sp³d hybridization — trigonal bipyramidal geometry.

diag.0: sp² gives 3 domains; PCl₅ has 5 bonded atoms.
diag.1: sp³ gives 4 domains.
diag.3: sp³d² gives 6 domains (octahedral).

why: Point P sits between the melting and vaporisation curves — moderate T and high enough P to keep matter in the liquid region.

why: At half-equivalence, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa — the flattest, most-buffered point on the curve.

diag.0: A is before any base has been added; that's just weak-acid pH, not a buffer mixture.
